name: ichiba.library.ref.sample
body:
A sample reference volume from the Ichiba library shelves.

Its pages describe the alchemical properties of common reagents found in the Maze.

name: ichiba.library.ref.wilds
body:
You find a good deal of material on the Second Realm, including the wastelands beyond the settled kingdoms. While the maps rarely agree on precise distances or borders, they consistently portray the wastelands as a place where the influence of the Maze is strongest, swallowing roads, isolating settlements and reshaping the land itself. 

Many works devote considerable space to the town of Hail, describing it as an important trading settlement and crossroads linking several Domains. Older editions speak warmly of its inns, markets and extensive library, while more recent works become noticeably scarce. None of the books expand on the town's sudden disappearance.

Several natural histories and explorers' journals describe the Stygios Forest as one of the oldest woodlands in the wastelands. The trees are said to grow unnaturally close together, allowing little sunlight to reach the forest floor, while fungi and decay dominate the undergrowth. Travellers consistently remark upon the forest's oppressive silence and the abundance of dangerous wildlife, leading many scholars to speculate that some malign influence has lingered there for centuries.

Accounts of Tornado Mountain are remarkably consistent despite the scarcity of expeditions. The summit is described as a barren landscape of shattered rock where fierce winds blow almost constantly, making travel hazardous even in fair weather.

The Writhing Mire is portrayed as a treacherous marsh where the landscape itself seems unwilling to remain fixed. Numerous travel journals complain of roads that vanish beneath stagnant water and pathways that appear only to disappear again hours later.

The books describe Hianbian less as a place than as a puzzle. Its countless corridors, chambers and identical doorways have defeated generations of cartographers, whose maps rapidly become contradictory. Several authors report inexplicable changes in orientation and impossible journeys between distant rooms, though none can explain the phenomenon satisfactorily.

Most scholars identify the Plain of Pillars as an ancient salt desert, distinguished by innumerable weathered stone columns rising from the barren ground. Their purpose is unknown. Archaeologists have proposed everything from forgotten monuments to boundary markers or the remains of a vanished civilisation, yet no convincing evidence has emerged in support of any theory.

The Caves of Ilast occupy surprisingly little space in the literature, perhaps because so few explorers have returned with reliable accounts. Those that have describe a subterranean labyrinth extending far beyond the areas that have been mapped. 

The Isle of the Gate occupies an unusual place in the historical record. Although outwardly described as peaceful and picturesque, nearly every account hints at a significance extending beyond its modest size. The island is repeatedly associated with ancient ruins and the all-important Gate to the Third Realm, prompting historians to speculate that it once served as a ceremonial or religious site. Frustratingly, the surviving records offer few details.
